Rooted in London · Serving Southwestern Ontario

You should not have to navigate Huntington disease alone.

Welcome to the Huntington Community of Southwestern Ontario (HCSWO) — connecting people, strengthening families, building community.

Our mission is to create a caregiver-centred, person- and family-focused community support bridge that connects people affected by Huntington disease with the services, information, and community supports they need to live well.

“Because no one should have to navigate Huntington disease alone.”

Short-Term Strategic Plan

Our five priorities for the next 12–24 months

Our objective is not to build a large service-delivery organisation, but to build the foundations of an effective local community-care bridge — and demonstrate that this approach works.

Trusted working relationships with the organisations most frequently needed — moving from informal knowledge toward documented, relationship-based referral pathways, including named organisational contacts, eligibility information, referral processes and follow-up. A clearer path to support: developing relationships with service providers so families can better understand where to turn, how to access assistance, and what to do next.
A practical navigation function helping individuals and caregivers understand available services, options, eligibility, and who to contact — and helping them take next steps. HCSWO functions as a connector rather than a case-management substitute. Personal connections between services: a referral should help someone reach support, with introductions, clear next steps and appropriate follow-up, with the person's consent.
Map existing resources across London and Southwestern Ontario, identify significant gaps and duplication, and translate specialist knowledge into accessible community resources for families and providers — progressively including a shared resource repository, educational sessions, referral tools and service maps. Knowledge people can use: reliable information made easier to find, understand and apply.
Caregiver needs should become a defining feature of the HCSWO model: caregiver information, navigation, peer and family connection, recognition of caregiver contributions, and support for transitions. HCSWO will not recreate existing caregiver services — its role is to identify, connect, adapt and supplement them where Huntington-specific gaps remain.
As the network matures, convene clinicians, community agencies, disease organisations and others to share learning, identify emerging needs and align local responses. A stronger local network: bringing people together across Southwestern Ontario to share knowledge and strengthen support.

HCSWO is developing these activities in stages as partnerships, funding, and capacity grow. Contact us to learn what is currently available.

A community built around people and families

Local focus. Shared knowledge. Stronger support.

Rooted in London and serving Southwestern Ontario, Canada, HCSWO connects people affected by Huntington disease with local services, information, navigation and referrals — and refers clinical, legal, financial or regulated issues to the appropriate professionals.

About Us & HD

Who we are — and what Huntington disease is

A caregiver-centred, person- and family-focused community support bridge for people affected by Huntington disease in Southwestern Ontario.

Our Mission

To create a caregiver-centred, person- and family-focused community support bridge that connects people affected by Huntington disease with the services, information, and community supports they need to live well.

Our Vision

A Southwestern Ontario community in which no individual or family affected by Huntington disease has to navigate the journey alone. Over time, HCSWO also seeks to demonstrate a locally grounded model that can inform broader cross-community care, including in rural and remote communities.

Understanding HD

What is Huntington disease (HD)?

HD is an inherited neurodegenerative disease affecting movement, thinking and emotions — and the lives of families and caregivers. It develops gradually over many years; early symptoms can be subtle and are often missed or attributed to stress, aging or other conditions. It affects everyone differently — symptoms and progression vary, and no two people experience it the same way.

Imagine facing the challenges of Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, ALS and schizophrenia — all at the same time. That's what Huntington's disease can be like.
HD affects everyone differently. While symptoms often include involuntary movements, cognitive changes, and emotional or behavioural changes, no two people experience it the same way. Symptoms can change over time, and the journey is unique for each person and family.
Because symptoms vary so widely, recognizing and understanding HD can be challenging, even for healthcare professionals.
Behind every diagnosis is a person, a family, and a story that deserves to be heard.
At the Huntington Community of Southwestern Ontario, we want to change silence into understanding, isolation into connection, and uncertainty into support.

HD and Genetics

Genetics, explained gently

HD is caused by a change in the HTT gene. A genetic test, usually using a blood sample, can identify whether a person carries the gene change that causes HD. Anyone considering testing is encouraged to speak with a genetic counsellor or healthcare professional.

Understanding Genetic Testing

A genetic test, usually using a blood sample, can identify whether a person carries the gene change that causes HD.

Huntington Society of Canada

Genetic Testing Is a Personal Choice

Choosing predictive genetic testing is an emotional and deeply personal decision; no one should feel pressured to be tested.

Huntington Society of Canada

The 50/50 Chance of Inheriting HD

If a parent carries the gene expansion, each child has a 50% chance of inheriting it — the same for sons and daughters, and each pregnancy is an independent risk.

Huntington Society of Canada

Getting Information and Support

Anyone considering testing is encouraged to speak with a genetic counsellor or healthcare professional for information and support.

Huntington Society of Canada

How We Help

We are a community in Southwestern Ontario dedicated to supporting individuals and families affected by Huntington disease. Our focus is to support you in addressing your needs by providing a bridge between the work being done across the health and social care system and the everyday realities families face. We strongly believe in collaborating with you and other organizations to manage both your immediate needs and long-term goals. Through stakeholder engagement, transparent plans and activities, accountability and striving every day to do better, we are building a community that listens, learns, and acts together.

Huntington disease is at the centre of our work. Where families affected by other neurological conditions face similar challenges, HCSWO will seek opportunities to learn and collaborate, while remaining accountable to its Huntington community.

SJ

Shelley-Ann John — DBA, MSc, PMP®

Shelley-Ann's background is in the rehabilitation sector, where she worked as a cognitive-behavioural therapist before moving into case management in Toronto personal-injury law firms, supporting clients with catastrophic injuries from motor-vehicle accidents. She owned a retail store and clinic with a multidisciplinary team, and specialised in behavioural medicine — non-medical approaches to chronic pain and mental-health challenges. She later served as Director, Strategy & Innovation for a family- and youth-centred clinic at the confluence of justice and mental health, and taught Business Strategy and Business Communication in the Master of Management and MBA programs at the University of Windsor. She holds a DBA from Athabasca University, an MSc in Behavioural Medicine, and a BSc in Psychology from McGill University, is a PMP® with the Project Management Institute, and is pursuing a Black Belt Certification in Lean Six Sigma. She is now a management consultant supporting non-profit, charitable and humanitarian organisations with strategic plans for sustainable social impact.

CG

Christina Galecki

Christina holds an Honours degree in Criminology from the University of Ottawa and a Master of Arts in Leadership from the University of Guelph's Gordon S. Lang School of Business and Economics. From 1998 to 2003 she was with the Department of Justice Canada as a Program Officer at the National Crime Prevention Centre, working on community mobilization and partnerships with nonprofits and the private sector through the Business Action Program. She recently retired after a 23-year career with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, with tactical and operational roles in Customs and Excise, Financial Crime, Drug Enforcement and National Security. She played a pivotal role establishing and advancing the Criminal Intelligence Program in the RCMP's Central Region and mentored dozens of intelligence analysts. She is an avid nature enthusiast, with a love of botany and wildlife.

BP

Barb Potempa

Barb brings a personal connection to Huntington disease, along with community advocacy and education. She is a volunteer and instructor with the Polish Scouting Association, working with children and youth on skills, confidence, leadership and Polish heritage and culture — and brings that same dedication to HD advocacy.

Families & Caregivers

Support for you, just as you are

It's ok to feel whatever you're feeling. There is no wrong way to feel about HD. You're not alone.

SadnessAngerGuiltFearReliefHopeExhaustionOverwhelmGriefLonelinessUncertainty

Your feelings matter. They are normal — and they deserve to be met with understanding, not fixing.

What helps, when you're ready

1

Give yourself permission to feel

Whatever you are feeling is valid. There is no wrong way to feel about HD.

2

Find one small anchor

A walk, a cup of tea, five minutes of quiet — one small thing that is just for you.

3

Let someone in

You don't have to carry this alone, and you don't have to explain everything.

4

Reach out when you need support

You deserve support just as much as the person you care for.

Here when you're ready

You don't have to know what to say or what you need. You only need to reach out. You don't have to do this alone.
